title: Gemini Nano on device — Florina Muntenescu & Oli Gaymond, Google DeepMind

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 86%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on ML Kit, AI Core, Firebase AI logic, and LiteRT as the developer platform and SDK substrate for building AI experiences on Android rather than a single end-user application. The subject matter is tools and platforms (ML Kit, AI Core, Firebase AI logic, LiteRT) used by software builders on Android. The talk covers building apps with GenAI APIs during development and AI Core's model serving, scheduling, and queuing during deployment. The session assumes developer familiarity and discusses practical tradeoffs like device reach, scheduling, hybrid inference, and battery impact. The session is a conference presentation with audience Q&A interspersed throughout. Eight evidence anchors with said_in_transcript grade directly support the key claims about AI Core sharing, scheduling, hybrid inference, device reach, and the coming embedding API.

summary: The talk covers three approaches to intelligent experiences on Android: on-device inference, hybrid inference, and cloud-only inference. On-device processing via ML Kit GenAI APIs gives developers access to Gemini Nano, Google's most efficient on-device model, which shares its architecture with Gemma 4 and is optimized for Android hardware. Gemini Nano is delivered through the AI Core system service, meaning one model is installed on the device and shared by all apps, avoiding the impracticality of each app shipping a 3-4 GB model. AI Core handles all scheduling: foreground apps get top priority, while background batch jobs are queued, often running overnight on charge. The developer never manages any of this. Requests run in isolation, and input/output data is never stored on device. The ML Kit GenAI suite includes task-specific APIs for summarization, proofreading, and rewrite, but the prompt API is the most flexible, accepting text and image input and returning text output, supporting use cases like image understanding, content assistance, and entity extraction. RAG-like solutions are possible with the prompt API today, and an embedding API is coming soon to make RAG easier. Gemini Nano is currently limited to flagship devices such as Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 class hardware and select OEMs. Classic ML Kit APIs for vision and OCR, by contrast, run on over a billion devices without issue. For broader reach with GenAI, hybrid inference was launched a couple of weeks before the talk via Firebase AI logic, automatically falling back to Gemini Flash in the cloud when on-device is unavailable. For fully custom models or wider device testing, LiteRT is the alternative path, but the developer must handle testing and optimization themselves. AI Edge Gallery serves as a showcase for frontier possibilities but requires more developer uplift, whereas AI Core is focused on easy production-level app building. During Q&A, the speakers clarify that the Gemini app and developer-facing on-device APIs are different user journeys, and that 'skills' are effectively composed into prompts rather than being a separate system feature.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Gemini Nano is delivered once per device through the AI Core system service and shared across all apps, avoiding the 3-4 GB per-app shipping problem.
AI Core handles all scheduling and queuing: foreground apps get top priority, background batch jobs queue and run overnight on charge, and the developer never manages any of it.
The ML Kit prompt API accepts text and image input and returns text output, supporting use cases like image understanding, content assistance, entity extraction, and RAG-style solutions.
An embedding API is coming soon, making RAG-like solutions easier to build with on-device Gemini embeddings.
Classic ML Kit APIs for vision and OCR run on over a billion devices, while GenAI APIs require recent flagship devices such as Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 generation hardware.
Hybrid inference via Firebase AI logic falls back to Gemini Flash in the cloud when on-device is unavailable, increasing feature reach.
LiteRT is the alternative for developers needing fully custom models or wider device testing, but requires the developer to handle testing and optimization themselves.

The Gemini app and developer-facing on-device APIs are separate user journeys; developers interact with the model through APIs, not the Gemini app.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Backgrounds
sections.summary: Florina Muntenescu introduces herself as a developer relations engineer working on AI intelligent experiences and developer productivity. Ollie introduces himself as PM for Android AI, covering everything from OS-level applied AI features like screen brightness and memory optimization, to developer tools, infrastructure, and low-level hardware acceleration with silicon partners. They invite audience questions throughout.

sections.title: Overview of Intelligent Experiences on Android
sections.summary: The speakers outline three approaches: on-device models, hybrid (on-device when available, cloud otherwise), and fully cloud inference. On-device processing keeps data on the device, enabling sensitive data handling, offline use, and zero inference cost. Two on-device paths exist: ML Kit GenAI APIs providing Gemini Nano, and LiteRT for custom models. A separate talk covers LiteRT.

sections.title: Gemini Nano and AI Core
sections.summary: Gemini Nano is Google's most efficient on-device model, sharing architecture with Gemma 4 and optimized for Android. It is delivered through the AI Core system service so one model is shared across all apps. The system optimizes for hardware, providing lower latency and faster execution. Requests run in isolation and input/output data is not stored on device, ensuring privacy and security.

sections.title: ML Kit GenAI APIs and Prompt API
sections.summary: ML Kit GenAI APIs are part of the broader ML Kit family, which also includes vision and natural language APIs. GenAI-specific APIs cover tasks like summarization, proofreading, and rewrite. The most powerful is the prompt API, which accepts natural language requests with text and image input and text output, supporting use cases such as image understanding, content assistance, content analysis, and entity extraction.

sections.title: Device Reach and Hybrid Inference
sections.summary: Gemini Nano is available only on flagship devices such as Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 generation and select OEMs. For broader reach, hybrid inference via Firebase AI logic was launched a couple of weeks before the talk, falling back to Gemini Flash in the cloud when on-device is unavailable. Firebase AI logic also provides access to more powerful cloud models (Pro, Flash, Flash Light) through the Gemini API and Vertex AI.

sections.title: Q&A: Battery and RAM Consumption
sections.summary: A question about RAM usage and battery consumption is addressed. Models require flagship capabilities. Battery impact exists if running non-stop, but typical interactive usage of 10-20 times per day is not concerning. Batch use cases are expected to run in the background, often overnight on charge. AI Core handles optimizations; custom model developers have profiling tools but must do their own optimization work.

sections.title: Q&A: Shared Model Scaling
sections.summary: A question about shared model scaling across potentially hundreds of apps is addressed. Models are 3-4 GB, impractical for per-app shipping. Centralizing via AI Core shares the cost once. The system manages queuing and battery attribution, similar to GPS or Wi-Fi. Users will spend battery on features they value; the platform makes capabilities available and lets developers build compelling features.

sections.title: Q&A: Scheduling and App Priority
sections.summary: AI Core handles all scheduling and queuing. Foreground apps get top priority, while background app requests are queued. Developers do not need to worry about scheduling logistics.

sections.title: Q&A: On-Device vs Cloud for Google Assistant and Skills
sections.summary: An audience member asks whether Google Assistant runs locally or remotely. The speakers clarify that the Gemini app and developer-facing on-device APIs are completely different user journeys. If you build your own app, you interact with the model directly through APIs, not through the Gemini app. Regarding 'skills,' the tools provided are low-level layers designed for developers or others to build on top of; skills are effectively composed into prompts, as tools like Pocket Claw or Open Claw would do.

sections.title: Q&A: RAG, Embeddings, and AI Edge Gallery
sections.summary: Gemini Nano is completely contained by AI Core with no setup or configuration needed from developers. RAG-like solutions are possible today with the prompt API, and an embedding API is coming soon to make RAG easier, using the Gemini embedding model. The prompt API can accept app-accessible files as input. AI Edge Gallery is a showcase for frontier possibilities but requires more developer uplift; AI Core is focused on easy, production-level app building where developers just focus on the prompt and feature.

sections.title: Q&A: Device and Model Matrix
sections.summary: A final question addresses the matrix of devices versus models. Classic ML Kit models (text, OCR, vision) are much smaller and run on over a billion devices without issue. GenAI APIs require fairly flagship devices from the last couple of years. AI Core guarantees things run well if covered. For wider device reach, LiteRT LM (covered in a separate talk by Cormac) can help, but the developer must handle testing themselves. The speakers close by inviting further questions today and tomorrow.

limitations: Gemini Nano is only available on recent flagship devices such as Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 class hardware and select OEMs.
Running Gemini Nano non-stop will drain the battery fairly quickly.
